FPG reductions were observed as early as Week 1 in alogliptin arms, and improvements in proinsulin/insulin ratio at Weeks 4 and 8 (p<0.05 vs placebo) and increased C-peptide at Week 8 (p=0.012) confirm DPP-4 inhibition is driving enhanced incretin-mediated insulin secretion. The dose-response relationship (12.5 mg: -4.7 mg/dL FPG; 25 mg: -8.4 mg/dL FPG vs placebo +2.2 mg/dL) further supports target engagement. 2. PATHWAY MODULATION: Downstream biology clearly moved. The proinsulin/insulin ratio decrease and C-peptide increase confirm that DPP-4 inhibition by alogliptin enhanced GLP-1-mediated insulin secretion (R-HSA-381676), consistent with the proposed mechanism. 3. CLINICAL TRANSLATION: The primary endpoint (HbA1c change at Week 26) was met for both doses: alogliptin 12.5 mg achieved -0.38% vs placebo +0.01% (p=0.001) and alogliptin 25 mg achieved -0.52% vs placebo +0.01% (p=0.001). Both are statistically significant and clinically meaningful in the context of add-on therapy to glyburide. A dose-response relationship is evident. 4. POPULATION EFFECTS: No subgroup analyses were reported. The enrolled population (T2DM inadequately controlled on sulfonylurea) is appropriate for the mechanism. 5. CONFOUNDERS: No major confounders identified. SAEs were infrequent and distributed across arms; no dose-limiting toxicity was observed. The modest weight gain in alogliptin arms (~0.8-0.9 kg) is a known class effect and did not compromise the trial. The 26-week duration is standard for HbA1c endpoint trials. Overall, this is a clean mechanistic success: target engaged, pathway modulated, clinical endpoint met with dose-response confirmation.
